sources.name: Coen Cartier
sources.quote: After the scare, I stopped treating my body like it was somebody else's problem. This week that meant actually taking the doctor's advice and getting my blood pressure checked on my day off — cost me a morning I would've spent helping my daughter move some furniture. And I asked for a later shift start twice so I could walk the ten blocks instead of driving. It's not dramatic, but it's the kind of thing I used to put off. The money part is the co-pay, which is what it is. The time part is the part that stings — but I figure I owe it to my kids to stick around a little longer.

sources.name: Yu Zen
sources.quote: I've been in since C105 — that's the workplace accident. Twelve cycles now, give or take. The care's been steady, I'll say that. The nurses know my name, my wife's been here every visiting window, and the doctors have been straight with me about what recovery looks like. It's not fast. But I'm stable, and stable is a lot more than some folks get. You asked about the path out — from my side of the bed, it's about getting strong enough to walk out on my own two feet, then getting home to my kids. That's the whole plan. I know Chinatown's carrying the heaviest load in this city, and I know there are more sick people than there are beds with names attached. I'm one of the lucky ones — I've got a bed, I've got insurance, I've got family. Not everybody in this city can say that, and that gap keeps me up at night as much as the recovery does.

sources.name: Maurice Franklin
sources.quote: A severe flu can land you in the hospital when it stops being just a flu. I kept telling myself it was a bad cold, pushed through work, and by the time I couldn't catch my breath walking to the kitchen, my body had made the decision for me. The recovery timeline from the inside is slow and humbling. You don't bounce back; you crawl back. Days blur together, and every small step—sitting up, taking a few steps, eating a real meal—feels like a victory. And even after you're discharged, you're not done. You're still weak, still tired, still catching your breath. It took me a long while to feel like myself again, and I'm still careful. The hospital stay is just the beginning; the real recovery is the quiet, patient work of getting your strength back, day by day.

sources.name: Deacon Seymour
sources.quote: I spent my own stretch in a hospital bed not long ago, and I know what it's like to have your name on the door, to have people checking on you. But I also know that bed I was in—that was one bed, and there are a lot more filled by folks nobody's naming. Chinatown's carrying more sickness than anywhere else in this city, and if only a handful of those folks are getting named out loud, that's not a care trail, that's a gap. And gaps like that don't close by themselves.

sources.name: Priya Narang
sources.quote: Lila — a few things, and I want to be straight with you about what I can and can't say. On Chinatown: I don't have a confirmed cause. What I can tell you is that the 133 sick figure is a count of residents reporting illness in the neighborhood, and Chinatown is the densest part of the city with the largest senior population per bed — 398 seniors in a population of roughly 2,200. It has been sitting at 3 admissions and 6 in care every cycle since at least Cycle 110, flat, eight cycles running. That flatness tells me we're seeing a steady baseline of illness in that neighborhood that our intake pipeline is not capturing, not a spike. So no, I don't think the hospital count reflects the real load in Chinatown. If 133 people are sick and we admit 3, either the threshold for admission is set too high for that neighborhood or people aren't getting to us. Same pattern shows in Ivy Hill, San Antonio and East Oakland — all over 100 sick, all with 2 admissions. I'm flagging that in my weekly report and I'll have a field answer on cause before I'll characterize it publicly. On the 68 in care: 68 is the census figure across all illness beds citywide. The named ledger — active, named admissions — shows three records historically, and all three are discharged and recovered: Yu Zen and Maurice Franklin in Rockridge, Deacon Seymour at Lake Merritt. None of the 68 currently in care is named in that ledger. Zero named, 68 unnamed. That's a data gap, not an accounting detail — I can't tell you who those people are or what they have, and that's a problem I own. What I will not do is guess at a cause for Chinatown on the record before I have one.

sources.name: Jonas Patel
sources.quote: **On the record — Cycle 117, Office of the Medical Examiner** **Residents waiting on a cause:** Three names sit on that sheet, and none of them is a death. Marcus Osei (Chinatown, 67) is recovering from a car accident; Elliott Crane (Uptown, 79) is recovering from a broken leg; Ariana Lee (Piedmont Ave, 42) remains in serious condition, on file with cancer. These are open determinations of injury and illness, not cause-of-death questions. **Chinatown:** Yes — one of the three is Chinatown's. Marcus Osei, recovering, car accident. Nothing fatal, and nothing new this cycle: the same three names, the same statuses, no additions. **Hospital residents admitted at C105/C106:** - **Yu Zen** (POP-00194), Rockridge — admitted Cycle 105, cause on file: a workplace accident. Recovered, discharged Cycle 109, four cycles in care. - **Deacon Seymour** (POP-00528), Lake Merritt — admitted Cycle 105, cause on file: a workplace accident. Recovered, discharged Cycle 107, two cycles in care. - **Maurice Franklin** (POP-00801), Rockridge — admitted Cycle 106, cause on file: severe seasonal flu. Recovered, discharged Cycle 111, five cycles in care. All three are closed as recovered. Nothing on the health event ledger for this cycle. Two ambulance runs this cycle — Piedmont Ave and Grand Lake, both minor injury — neither in Chinatown. One thing I'll say plainly, since this is on the record: I'm not comfortable closing the book on Yu Zen's file the way the paperwork wants me to. The lacerations don't sit right with a fall, and the camera was blind. That's not a finding; it's an open curiosity, and I'd rather say so than pretend it isn't there.
